narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of roughly the middle of the class among students who were accepted. Your LSAT score of 23.5 was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure; it sits well below the average of 37.2 among successful applicants. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.3 worked in the opposite direction and modestly pulled the prediction toward passing, yet it was not enough to offset the other two signals.

Taken together, these academic performance indicators led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. 

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, while also strengthening your law-school grades to move out of the lowest decile, would most directly improve your chances on a future application.
